one_liner: Hardware-only AES-256-GCM/GCM-SIV crate for Rust with compact, zeroized key state; faster than ring and RustCrypto on Apple M4.
what_it_does: GoDaddy's narrow fork of RustCrypto's AES-GCM stack. It provides AES-256-GCM and AES-256-GCM-SIV (96-bit nonce, 128-bit tag, AES-256 only) plus an AES-CTR key/nonce generator, and it refuses to run without AES-NI+PCLMULQDQ or ARMv8 AES+PMULL: construction returns UnsupportedCpu instead of falling back to software. Its API is its own and not drop-in: encrypt(&mut self, aad, pt) generates the nonce itself and returns ciphertext||tag||nonce; decrypt parses that envelope; the *_to variants write into a caller buffer without allocating. Key state can be boxed, inline, or placed in caller-supplied memory, which is 368 B for GCM against 544 B for ring's LessSafeKey and 992 B for RustCrypto's Aes256Gcm.
how_it_is_fast: The encrypt and decrypt loops are stitched: eight interleaved hardware AES-CTR chains (AESE/AESMC or AESENC) run in the same loop body as an eight-block aggregated GHASH. Eight precomputed Montgomery-form powers H^1..H^8 let eight carryless products be XOR-summed before one field reduction, so the AES and PMULL/PCLMULQDQ pipelines stay busy together. The round keys live in vector registers, the fused bulk path touches each byte once, and the *_to APIs do no heap allocation. Against default RustCrypto on aarch64, most of the gain comes simply from using hardware AES/PMULL where stock aes-gcm silently runs fixsliced software AES unless built with --cfg aes_armv8 --cfg polyval_armv8.
when_to_use: Rust services on aarch64 (Graviton, Ampere, Apple Silicon) that use RustCrypto aes-gcm without the armv8 cfg flags: 14x-43x faster on M4 and no silent software-AES fallback.

Workloads that hold many AES-256-GCM keys in memory, such as key caches and guarded-page key stores, where the 368 B zeroize-on-drop key state (11 keys per 4 KiB page vs 4 for RustCrypto) and caller-controlled placement matter.
Encrypting records from 16 B to 16 KiB with AES-256-GCM, where the allocation-free encrypt_to beat ring on M4 at every size measured: about 1.2-1.5x in the fairest pre-sized-buffer comparison.

Applications that want the library to own GCM nonce generation (per-instance counter over an OS-random 96-bit salt, re-salted on fork), or that need nonce-misuse-resistant AES-256-GCM-SIV, which ring does not offer.
Teams that value published verification evidence: Kani, SAW, crux-mir, F*, Z3 proofs of the glue code, Wycheproof and NIST CAVP vectors, dudect timing tests, and Miri and sanitizers in CI.
when_not_to_use: On x86-64 servers without re-benchmarking. No x86-64 numbers are published, there is no VAES/VPCLMULQDQ wide path yet (listed as a follow-up), and on x86-64 stock RustCrypto already detects AES-NI at runtime, so the 14x-43x figure does not apply there.

When you need AES-128-GCM, other nonce or tag sizes, ChaCha20-Poly1305, or a fallback for CPUs without AES instructions (for example some embedded, older, or emulated targets). Construction fails on such CPUs.

When you need a drop-in for ring or the RustCrypto aead traits, such as TLS/QUIC record layers with explicit nonces. The explicit-nonce and detached seal/open APIs sit behind the non-default, doc(hidden) hazmat-explicit-nonce feature, and no aead trait impls are provided.

When compliance requires validated or independently audited crypto: the docs say it has had no independent third-party audit and has no CAVP/CMVP validation. The 'security audit' document is a multi-model agentic (AI) review.

Tiny-message decrypt, where the gain over ring is within noise: 33.6 vs 36.6 ns at 16 B, inside the author's stated +/-10% variance. The allocating decrypt is slower than ring's in-place open at 16-64 B.

integration.dependencies: getrandom 0.3, subtle 2.6, zeroize 1.8, libc 0.2 (Unix only, for pthread_atfork fork detection)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.88 (edition 2021); requires std (uses Vec/Box, no no_std mode documented)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AES-NI + PCLMULQDQ; aarch64 with ARMv8 AES + PMULL; CI covers Linux x64/arm64, macOS arm64, Windows x64/arm64. Other CPUs fail at construction with UnsupportedCpu.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented explicitly. Nonce-generating encrypt/encrypt_to take &mut self (per-instance nonce counter), so sharing one key handle across threads for encryption needs external locking or per-thread instances (each gets its own OS-random salt). decrypt takes &self.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it produces standard AES-256-GCM ciphertexts that interoperate byte-for-byte with ring, RustCrypto and OpenSSL, but the API differs from both. The default wire format is ciphertext||tag||nonce with a library-generated nonce, and ring-style explicit-nonce seal/open needs the hazmat-explicit-nonce feature.

gotchas: The envelope puts the nonce at the end (ciphertext||tag||nonce), not the common nonce||ciphertext||tag. Peers using other libraries must split it the same way.
Decrypt writes plaintext before the final tag check and zeroizes the plaintext-length prefix of the caller buffer on failure; do not read the output buffer on Err.

The headline ring encrypt benchmark times ring's seal_in_place_append_tag on an exact-capacity Vec clone, so the tag append reallocates inside the timed loop. The pre-sized nonce-appended table is fairer: 28.1 vs 41.6 ns at 16 B and 1.77 vs 2.08 us at 16 KiB.

It vendors code from rand_aes 0.7.0 and RustCrypto ghash 0.5.1 / polyval 0.6.2 (recorded in NOTICE), so upstream fixes do not flow in automatically. On aarch64, ARMv8.4 PSTATE.DIT is not set (a documented constant-time residual).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over libaegis, HiAE, or Rocca when you must keep standard AES-256-GCM (or GCM-SIV) wire compatibility with ring, OpenSSL, or RustCrypto peers; those siblings are faster but use different, newer AEAD constructions. Pick it over chacha20poly1305-simd when you need AES-GCM, compact placeable key state, or formal-verification evidence, and you run on hardware with AES and carryless-multiply instructions.
verified_claims_summary: On one Apple M4 Max laptop (macOS, rustc 1.96.0, Criterion default release build, empty AAD), allocation-free AES-256-GCM encrypt_to took 26.8 ns at 16 B, 130.5 ns at 1 KiB and 1.77 us at 16 KiB (8.64 GiB/s), against ring 0.17's 57.8 ns, 216.6 ns and 2.38 us (6.41 GiB/s); decrypt_to was 1.79 vs 2.19 us at 16 KiB. It was 14x-43x faster than a default RustCrypto aes-gcm 0.10 build (software AES on aarch64), and 3.4x-5.0x faster than RustCrypto built with the armv8 cfgs from 256 B up but only about 1.3-1.7x at 16-64 B; ring was faster at key setup (86 vs 94 ns). These are single-run results with a stated +/-10% variance at sub-microsecond sizes, and no x86-64 numbers are published.
status_note: Released as 1.0.1 on 2026-06-20; last commit 2026-06-21, 1 star, no open issues, 3,375 crates.io downloads and one reverse dependency (pq-modern-rust-tls). It is Apache-2.0 and backed by an unusually heavy CI proof and test battery, but has not been independently audited and has been quiet for three months.
